title: Your first C program
objective: By the end of this lesson you can write, compile, and run a C program that takes input and produces output, and you can read every line of it without guessing.

blocks.caption: greet.c — every part explained below
lines: int main(void) {            /* the program starts here */
return 0;               /* 0 means success, as in the shell */

items: Every statement ends with a semicolon; blocks are wrapped in braces
Every variable declares its type, and the type never changes
main returns int — the exit code the shell reads, which you met in the Linux course
Text in double quotes is a string; single quotes are one character: 'a' is not "a"

blocks.text: The types you will actually use

rows: One byte — a character or a small number
A number with a fractional part
A size or count — never negative

blocks.title: Sizes are not guaranteed, which matters more than it sounds
blocks.text: The standard specifies minimums, not exact sizes. Code that assumes int is 4 bytes can break when moved to a different platform. When the size matters — a network protocol, a file format, anything crossing a boundary — use the explicit types from <stdint.h>: int32_t, uint64_t, and so on. sizeof tells you the truth on the machine you are on.
printf: the format string is a small language

blocks.title: A wrong format specifier is undefined behaviour, not a display bug
blocks.text: printf trusts the format string completely: it reads arguments according to what you wrote there. Passing a long where %d is expected, or forgetting an argument entirely, makes it read whatever happens to be in that position. This is why -Wall matters — the compiler checks format strings against their arguments and will tell you.

blocks.caption: Two ways, one of which is safe
lines: gets(line);                       /* removed from the language — never use it */
if (fgets(line, sizeof line, stdin) != NULL) {   /* bounded: cannot overflow */
if (scanf("%d", &n) == 1) {       /* always check the return value */

blocks.title: Why gets was deleted from the language
blocks.text: It read input into a buffer with no way to specify the buffer's size — so any input longer than the buffer wrote past the end of it. That single function was behind a long list of exploited vulnerabilities, and the standards committee eventually removed it. fgets takes a size, which is the entire difference.

blocks.title: Write, break, and fix a program
steps: Create greet.c with the first example above
Change %d to %s in the printf and rebuild — read the warning carefully, then run it
Fix it, then add: printf("int is %zu bytes\n", sizeof(int));
Rewrite main as int main(int argc, char *argv[]) and print every argument
Replace the greeting name with input read using fgets
blocks.expected: A program you wrote from scratch, a deliberate format-string mistake that the compiler warned you about before it could misbehave, the real size of an int on your machine, and command-line arguments printed back. Notice that -Wall caught the mistake at compile time — that is the habit worth keeping.

cheatsheet: int main(void) or int main(int argc, char *argv[]); return 0 means success
Every variable has a declared type; every statement ends in a semicolon
"text" is a string, 'x' is a single character — they are different things
Sizes are not guaranteed: use <stdint.h> types when the size matters, and sizeof to check
printf: %d int · %ld long · %zu size_t · %f double · %s string · %c char · %p address
A mismatched format specifier is undefined behaviour — -Wall catches it
Never use gets; fgets(buf, sizeof buf, stdin) takes a size and cannot overflow
Always check the return value of scanf and fgets
argv[0] is the program name; real arguments start at argv[1]

checkpoint.prompt: What does return 0 from main mean?

choices.B: It is the exit code: 0 means success, non-zero means failure — the same convention the shell uses
choices.D: It is required syntax with no meaning

checkpoint.explanation: It is the same exit code you read with echo $? in the shell, which is how scripts and CI know whether your program succeeded.

checkpoint.prompt: Why was gets removed from the C standard?

choices.B: It had no way to limit how much it read, so any input longer than the buffer wrote past the end of it

checkpoint.explanation: A function that cannot be used safely regardless of caller care. fgets takes a size, which is the whole difference.

checkpoint.prompt: You write printf("%d\n", someLongValue) where the value is a long. What is the situation?

choices.A: It prints the value correctly; C converts automatically
choices.B: It is undefined behaviour — printf reads the argument according to the format string, so the output may be wrong or worse

checkpoint.explanation: printf trusts the format string. -Wall checks format strings against their arguments, which is why the warnings are worth turning on.

checkpoint.prompt: Why should you use <stdint.h> types like uint32_t when the size matters?

choices.B: Because the standard only specifies minimum sizes, so int can differ between platforms — explicit types keep the layout the same everywhere

checkpoint.explanation: Anything crossing a boundary — a file format, a network protocol, shared memory — needs a layout that does not depend on which machine compiled the code.
